strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: automatic generation of agent evaluation tasks, going beyond static/manual benchmarks, with a unified knowledge-graph-based abstraction that supports both document comprehension and web interaction tasks.

The design is reasonably complete and well-motivated: KG construction from parsed documents and crawled web pages, subgraph sampling with task templates and meta-paths, a multi-stage filtering/coverage-optimization pipeline (quality scoring, MMR-based diversity selection), and end-to-end evaluation across multiple agent types (Single, Multi-Agent, SoM, Agent S 2.5).

Concrete instantiation and broad experiments: Graph2Eval-Bench with 1,319 tasks (1,002 doc / 317 web) over 16 documents and 8 websites, evaluated with 7 model families and 4 agent architectures; the experiments do show the benchmark discriminates across models and agent scales (e.g., Table 2, Table 3), and the finding that multi-agent collaboration increases token cost without improving doc comprehension is a useful, non-trivial observation.

The claim of being the first framework to automatically generate interactive web tasks from crawled pages (seed-driven sampling + graph-regex meta-paths) is a genuine differentiator relative to TaskCraft-style text-only generation, and appendices A–G provide substantial implementation detail (metrics formulas, judge prompts, template and meta-path design, agent architectures, case study), supporting reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: Task correctness and answer validity are not independently verified. Gold answers for generated tasks appear to be produced by LLMs (Jinja2 reference-answer templates + GPT-4o generation). There is no human verification study, no estimate of the fraction of tasks with incorrect/unanswerable gold answers, and no inter-annotator agreement. Since both task generation and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring likely share the same backbone model family, correlated errors could systematically bias the reported model rankings.

The LLM-as-a-Judge success metric for web tasks (and judge scoring for doc tasks) is not validated against human judgments or programmatic ground truth; for web tasks the framework abandons rule-based checking entirely in favor of an LLM evaluator, and no measurement of judge reliability (e.g., agreement with manual labels on a sample) is reported. This is a material gap for a paper whose central claim is about evaluation reliability.

The core motivation—avoiding contamination/memorization from static data—is undermined by the data sources: doc tasks are generated from well-known recent papers (GPT-4o System Card, DeepSeek-R1, TaskCraft, AgentHarm, o3/o4-mini, Qwen-VL), whose contents frontier models have likely seen in pretraining. The paper does not measure or discuss this contamination risk, nor does it compare against memorized behavior on the same documents.

No baselines or ablations for the generation pipeline itself. There is no comparison against alternative automatic task generation (e.g., TaskCraft, Self-Instruct-style expansion) on the same data sources, and none of the claimed design choices (motif/centrality/semantic/hybrid sampling, MMR coverage optimization, filtering stages) are ablated. The efficiency claim (34.87s/95.51s per task) is only compared informally to 'manual construction' without quantification.

Scale and distribution concerns: only 16 documents and 8 websites; web task types are highly skewed (194/317 business_search_filter, a single toast_notification task), and live-website evaluation raises reproducibility and reliability questions (page drift), which the paper acknowledges only implicitly. Many web success rates are near zero for SoM Agent, suggesting tasks may be too hard or judge/instrumentation issues rather than informative difficulty.

Presentation quality is below the bar in places: duplicated and near-identical Appendices B and C on task templates; typos throughout ('Furturemore', 'gemini-2.5-falsh', 'typies', 'Role Defination', 'difficluty' in Figure 2); inconsistent bold/underline marking in Tables 2–3 (e.g., underlined 0.6250 not second-best); Figure 1's captionless panel 'Agent S 2.5'; the abstract's code link is a placeholder ('available here'); Figure 9's caption ('Case study') does not match its content. These are correctable but suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

The multi-agent architecture is evaluated only on doc tasks and the conclusion that multi-agent collaboration is unhelpful is drawn from one specific 5-role RAG pipeline; this finding may be an artifact of the chosen architecture rather than a property of the benchmark, and should be more carefully caveated.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and timely: using a knowledge graph as a 'latent task space' from which multimodal document-comprehension and web-interaction agent tasks are sampled via meta-paths and subgraph sampling, is a coherent and reasonably novel framing for automatic agent benchmark construction.

The framework covers the full lifecycle (parsing, KG construction, sampling, generation, filtering/coverage optimization) and supports heterogeneous agent types (single, multi-agent, SoM, Agent S 2.5), which is more end-to-end than many prior synthetic-task efforts limited to text QA.

The evaluation spans many model families and scales (GPT-4o/4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V3/V3.1, Qwen2.5-VL 7B/32B/72B, Gemini-2.5-flash) and both generation-time and discriminative-power analyses are reported, with appendices providing templates, meta-path design, agent architectures, and prompts that aid reproducibility of the pipeline.
The finding that multi-agent collaboration increases token cost without improving RAG-based document comprehension is a useful, clearly stated empirical observation.
weaknesses: Contamination undermines the paper's own core motivation. The introduction argues static benchmarks fail because models memorize training data, yet the document tasks are built from widely circulated arXiv papers (GPT-4o System Card, DeepSeek-R1, TaskCraft, OS Agents, Qwen-VL, etc.) that are almost certainly in the pretraining corpora of the evaluated models. The paper neither analyzes nor mitigates this, which directly conflicts with the claimed benefit over static datasets.

Task and answer quality are not validated against human judgment. Gold answers are produced by LLMs and success is judged by LLM-as-a-judge, with GPT-4o serving both as the primary task generator and (for web tasks, e.g., Figure 10) the validation model. This creates a potential generator/judge circularity and self-preference bias, and there is no human verification, no agreement statistics, and no calibration of judge reliability to support the reported scores.

The scale and balance of Graph2Eval-Bench is thin: only 16 documents and 8 websites produce 1,319 tasks, and the web-task distribution is severely skewed (194 business_search_filter vs. 1 toast_notification task). Category-level web results (e.g., Table 3) are therefore computed on a handful of tasks per cell, making scores like 0.0000 or 1.0000 statistically fragile; no confidence intervals or per-category task counts are given alongside results.

Web evaluation is performed on live websites (wired.com, The Guardian, GitHub, etc.), which threatens both reproducibility and correctness of the benchmark over time: page content, layout, and element availability change, and the LLM-judged success criterion is tied to volatile page state. No snapshot/frozen-environment strategy is reported.

The claim of being 'the first framework capable of automatically generating interactive tasks in web environment' is an overclaim given prior automated web-agent task/environment construction efforts (e.g., WebArena-style task synthesis, AgentTrek-style synthesis from web corpora), which the related-work section does not clearly differentiate or empirically compare against; there is no head-to-head comparison with TaskCraft or other synthetic-task generators to substantiate the claimed advantages.

Evidence that the benchmark measures 'reasoning, collaboration, and interaction capabilities' is indirect: the paper shows models differ in scores, but differentiating models is a weak validity criterion; no correlation with established benchmarks (GAIA, OSWorld, WebArena) or ablations linking task structure (subgraph hops, meta-path type) to measured capability is provided. The claimed 'controllable complexity' is never empirically demonstrated.

Presentation is noticeably rough for a submission: typos ('Furturemore', 'typies', 'Defination', 'difficluty', 'gemini-2.5-falsh'), a placeholder code link ('Our code is available here:' with no URL), a Figure 9 caption describing a case study while the figure shows task-type distributions, duplicated task-template content between Appendices B and C, and 'Agent S 2.5' results that appear inconsistent with the cited Agent S paper. These issues, while individually minor, collectively suggest insufficient polish.
The safety-task extension (Appendix H) is described but not evaluated with any experiments, adding length without evidence.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: scalable, automated generation of evaluation tasks for multimodal agents, moving beyond static hand-annotated benchmarks.

The knowledge-graph-as-latent-task-space formulation is a sensible and reasonably original design: nodes/edges encode both semantic and interactive elements, and subgraph sampling + task templates + meta-paths provide a structured mechanism for controlling task complexity (Algorithm 1, meta-path patterns in Appendix D).

The framework is broad in scope: it supports document comprehension tasks, multi-step web interaction tasks, and multiple agent configurations (Single, Multi, SoM, Agent S 2.5), with a concrete instantiation (Graph2Eval-Bench, 1,319 tasks) and reported generation-time efficiency (Fig. 5).

The coverage optimization stage (quality scoring, MMR-based selection, multi-dimensional coverage in Fig. 4) shows awareness of diversity/representativeness issues that plague synthetic task generation.

The experimental findings are plausible and useful, e.g., multi-agent collaboration increases token cost without improving document comprehension (Table 2), and clear capability gaps across model scales and agent types (Tables 2-3).

The appendices provide useful implementation detail: metric formulas and judge prompts (Appendix A), template structure (B-C), meta-path design with a graph regex engine (D), dataset composition (E), and agent architectures (F).
weaknesses: Circularity in task/ground-truth construction is the most material concern: GPT-4o generates the tasks and the gold answers, and evaluation of the same/competing models relies heavily on LLM-as-a-judge (with GPT-4o as judge/validator). No human verification of task correctness, answer validity, or judge agreement is reported, so the benchmark may systematically favor models similar to the generator/judge. This undermines the paper's own motivation about disentangling true capability from memorization.

No ablation studies. The pipeline has many components (multi-stage filtering, node reachability, similarity-based novelty, MMR selection, sampling strategies, meta-path tiers), but there is no evidence of which contribute to task quality or discriminative power. Claims like 'guarantee the quality and executability of the generated tasks' are not substantiated with controlled comparisons.

Limited scale and questionable statistical support: only 16 documents and 8 websites; web task types have very small samples (e.g., toast_notification n=1, modal_interaction n=6 in Fig. 9), making Table 3 cell values (e.g., 1.0000 or 0.0000) statistically meaningless; no confidence intervals, seeds, or variance over repeated agent runs are reported, despite live-web stochasticity.

The live-website dependency (crawling and executing on WIRED, GitHub, OpenWeather, etc.) raises serious reproducibility concerns: pages change or break over time, and the paper does not describe snapshots, caching, or controlled replay environments. Code is claimed to be 'available here:' but no actual link is provided.

The novelty claim 'the first framework capable of automatically generating interactive tasks in web environment' is overclaimed relative to cited related work (TaskCraft, WebArena-style automated setups) and needs qualification; the related-work positioning of Section 2 is somewhat superficial and does not clearly differentiate Graph2Eval from TaskCraft's document-traversal-based task expansion.

Domain narrowness contradicts the stated motivation: document tasks are drawn from AI research papers (mostly arXiv-adjacent content, Appendix E), so strong models may partially answer from pretraining knowledge - exactly the memorization confound the introduction criticizes. No experiment checks this (e.g., answering without document access).

The claimed contributions about measuring 'collaboration' capabilities are weakly supported: the multi-agent system is a single fixed architecture (planner/retriever/reasoner/verifier/summarizer), and the finding that it degrades performance suggests the collaboration evaluation is thin rather than that the benchmark measures collaboration in general.

Numerous presentation flaws that suggest limited polish: typos ('Furturemore', 'typies', 'Defination', 'difficluty', 'gemini-2.5-falsh'), Fig. 9's caption does not match its content (it shows task-type distributions, not a case study), Appendix E references 'Table 8' that does not exist, and the abstract's code link is empty.
Appendix H (safety task generation) is exploratory with no quantitative results or evaluation, and its inclusion as a contribution direction dilutes rather than strengthens the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: automated, scalable generation of agent evaluation tasks, and it offers a unifying framework spanning both RAG/document-understanding agents and web agents, which most prior synthesis methods (e.g., TaskCraft, Learn-by-interact) do not.

The core idea of treating a knowledge graph built from heterogeneous sources as a structured 'task space' with template- and meta-path-guided subgraph sampling is a sensible and reasonably novel mechanism for grounding generated tasks in verifiable data relationships, directly targeting semantic consistency and solvability.

The pipeline is described in reasonable technical detail (KG construction, node/edge typing, Algorithm 1 for subgraph sampling, coverage optimization via MMR, meta-path patterns in Appendix C), and the safety/filtering constraints in Appendix A are thoughtfully specified.

A concrete benchmark (Graph2Eval-Bench, 1,319 tasks) is instantiated and evaluated with multiple agent architectures (single/multi-agent RAG, SoM, Agent S 2.5) and many foundation models, and the benchmark does appear to discriminate performance (Table 3 shows clear gaps, e.g., Agent S 2.5 at 0.692 vs. SoM at 0.145 on Gemini 2.5 Flash).

An ablation against a KG-free variant with both human and agent evaluation (Table 4) supports the central claim that KG grounding improves consistency and solvability, and limitations are honestly discussed (Appendix D).
weaknesses: Potential circularity in evaluation: GPT-4o is used for task generation, filtering, LLM-as-a-Judge scoring of document tasks, and web success-rate judgments, while task quality claims (consistency/solvability) rest largely on LLM judgments of GPT-4o-generated tasks. The LLM-judge reliability check (Appendix F.3) is based on only 50 trajectories from a single agent with 88% agreement, which is a thin validation for the benchmark's primary web metric.

Scale and coverage of the benchmark are limited: 16 documents and 8 websites yield 1,319 tasks, with highly skewed distributions (e.g., business_search_filter 194 vs. toast_notification 1, modal_interaction 6). Per-cell results in Table 3 for rare task types (e.g., 1.0000 SR on toast tasks) are statistically unreliable, and the human evaluation sample sizes for the ablation are not reported.

Graph quality verification is shallow: KG edge precision is estimated from only 100 randomly sampled node pairs (88%), yet the entire approach's quality hinges on graph correctness; no sensitivity analysis of task quality to graph errors is provided despite this being the acknowledged main limitation.

Comparisons with existing methods are largely qualitative: Tables 5 and 6 compare against OSWorld, MMBench, and TaskCraft using generic descriptors (e.g., 'High/Moderate/Low' time cost, methodology labels) rather than head-to-head empirical generation comparisons; only the KG-free variant is empirically ablated.

The headline claims of '20% semantic consistency and 17% solvability improvement' derive from a single ablation with two annotators and unclear sample size, and doc-task improvements in Table 4 are smaller than the abstract implies (consistency 0.74→0.95, solvability 0.73→0.93 for doc, but web consistency only 0.62→0.78), suggesting the web scenario—arguably the harder and more novel setting—benefits less.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the Project Page is empty, no code or data release is stated, and many implementation details (prompt templates for generation, the Graph Regex Engine, sampling hyperparameters τ and k) are only described at a high level, making the framework difficult for others to reproduce or extend.

Live-website task generation and evaluation raise practical concerns (page drift, site changes between generation and evaluation, robots/compliance) that are mentioned but not analyzed; the paper does not report how many tasks failed at execution time due to environment changes.

strengths: The core idea of treating a knowledge graph built from heterogeneous sources (documents + crawled web pages) as a structured 'task space' for agent evaluation is a reasonable and somewhat novel perspective, and it is implemented end-to-end across both RAG and Web agent scenarios (GRAPH2EVAL-BENCH with 1,319 tasks).

The ablation in Table 4 directly addresses the central claim: removing the KG degrades human-judged consistency (e.g., 0.95→0.74 doc, 0.78→0.62 web) and solvability (0.93→0.73 doc, 0.72→0.60 web), and widens performance gaps across model scales, providing concrete, if limited, evidence for the KG's value.

The multi-stage filtering pipeline (reachability analysis, LLM scoring, MMR-based novelty/coverage selection) is a sensible engineering contribution, and the paper reports generation efficiency (~35s/document task, ~96s/web task) and a modest but honest safety/ethics discussion (Appendix A), including a preliminary safety-task generation extension (Appendix I).

Evaluating multiple model families (GPT, DeepSeek, Qwen-VL, Gemini, UI-TARS) across four agent architectures gives a reasonable breadth of discriminative analysis, and the Agent S 2.5 vs. SoM Agent gap (69.2% vs. 14.5%) supports the claim that the tasks measure multi-step reasoning rather than simple visual grounding.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth and statistical support are thin. The benchmark is built from only 16 documents and 8 websites; web task types are severely imbalanced (Figure 4: 194 'business_search_filter' vs. 1 'toast_notification'), and several Table 3 cells (e.g., Toast success rates of 1.0) are computed from a handful of tasks, likely 1–6, making many reported numbers statistically meaningless. No variance, confidence intervals, or per-task counts are given.

The headline claims of '20% semantic consistency and 17% solvability improvements' rest on a single human evaluation with only two annotators, no reported inter-annotator agreement, and no description of how many tasks were rated. The LLM-judge reliability check (Appendix F.3) itself shows only 88% agreement with humans on 50 sampled trajectories — an 12% error rate on the very metric (SR) used for all web results — which is not convincingly validated as 'high consistency.'

The KG Edge Precision is only 88% (Table 1), yet the paper's core argument is that the KG enforces semantic correctness and solvability. The paper does not analyze how the ~12% erroneous edges propagate into the 1,319 released tasks or affect solvability, leaving a tension between the stated motivation and the reported quality.

The comparison with prior work (Section 4.4, Tables 5 and 6) is purely qualitative — feature checklists rather than head-to-head task generation against the named baselines (OSWorld, MMBench, TaskCraft). Given that TaskCraft [29] is the closest method and is cited extensively, an empirical comparison of generated-task quality would be expected and its absence weakens the contribution claims.

The pipeline is heavily dependent on the very LLMs it aims to evaluate: GPT-4o performs task generation, filtering, and scoring, and GPT-4o is also the web-task success judge. This creates both a potential circularity/self-preference bias (GPT-4o-based generation judged by GPT-4o) and reproducibility concerns for a closed-source, evolving model.

Reproducibility is not established. The 'Project Page' field on the title page is empty, no code or data release is stated, and key components (StructMatch, the Graph Regex Engine, meta-path templates, agent hyperparameters) are deferred to an appendix that provides only high-level descriptions. The web tasks depend on live crawled websites, which change over time and would make results non-reproducible without released snapshots.

Presentation issues undermine clarity: Algorithm 1 is essentially trivial (threshold or k-hop filtering) relative to the elaborate formalism; Figure 2 is dense and hard to parse; the citations include a duplicated entry ([38]/[39] are identical OSWorld citations) and a 2026-dated reference, suggesting insufficient proofreading. The paper also asserts that KG-based generation is 'reproducible' without demonstrating determinism given stochastic LLM generation.

The claimed novelty over TaskCraft and Learn-by-interact [31] is incremental: the differentiator is mainly that tasks are grounded in a graph, but the graph itself is constructed with LLM extraction and the tasks are ultimately produced by LLM prompting over subgraphs — so the KG acts as structured conditioning rather than a fundamentally different generation mechanism, which the ablation supports but does not establish as a general advance.

strengths: Addresses a real and timely problem: scalable, contamination-resistant task generation for evaluating multimodal LLM agents, unifying RAG (document understanding) and web interaction scenarios in a single KG-based framework.

The KG-as-task-space idea is a sensible mechanism for grounding generated tasks in verifiable entity/relation structure, and the full pipeline (ingestion → KG construction → subgraph sampling → templated generation → MMR-based coverage optimization) is described at a level of detail sufficient to understand and potentially reimplement, with substantial supporting material (templates, meta-paths, agent architectures, prompts) in the appendices.

The core ablation (Table 4) provides quantitative evidence for the KG's value: human-evaluated consistency (0.95 vs 0.74 doc; 0.78 vs 0.62 web) and solvability (0.93 vs 0.73; 0.72 vs 0.60) improve substantially over the KG-free variant, corroborated by agent evaluations showing clearer model-size separation.

Breadth of downstream validation: 10+ models across GPT, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemini, and UI-TARS families, and two agent paradigms (RAG single/multi-agent; SoM and Agent S 2.5 web agents), showing the benchmark discriminates performance scales and architectures (e.g., the Agent S 2.5 vs SoM gap on Gemini 2.5 Flash).

The LLM-as-judge success metric is at least partially validated against human annotations (88% agreement on 50 sampled trajectories), and the safety/filtering constraints in Appendix A show attention to responsible web data collection.
weaknesses: Comparisons with related work are largely qualitative rather than empirical. Tables 5 and 6 (vs OSWorld, MMBench, TaskCraft) are feature-comparison matrices, not head-to-head task-quality experiments on the same data. The headline claims of +20% consistency and +17% solvability rest solely on the internal KG-free ablation with two annotators, whose scoring procedure ('proportion of cases where both annotators reached agreement') is ambiguous and lacks inter-annotator statistics or significance testing.

Scale and diversity of Graph2Eval-Bench are thin: only 16 documents and 8 websites, with 83.5 tasks per document (raising redundancy questions despite the MMR novelty filter). Web-side per-category sample sizes are extremely small (toast_notification n=1, modal_interaction n=6), which makes several per-category entries in Table 3 (e.g., SR of 1.0000 for Toast) statistically uninformative and undermines claims that the benchmark reliably differentiates models.

Constructed KG quality is imperfect (88% edge precision from a 100-pair manual check), meaning ~12% of edges are erroneous; the paper does not analyze how these errors propagate into unsolvable or inconsistent tasks, despite acknowledging this dependence in Appendix D.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge for web task success and for consistency/novelty scoring introduces circularity concerns, especially since GPT-4o is also used for task generation; the human validation covers only 50 of 317 web trajectories.

The central motivation—avoiding memorization/contamination—is partially self-undermined: 14 of the 16 document sources are well-known public arXiv papers (GPT-4o system card, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-VL, OS Agents, TaskCraft, etc.) that are almost certainly in the pretraining corpora of the evaluated models. Additionally, live-website crawling (8 sites) poses reproducibility and temporal-validity problems; no snapshotting or frozen-environment strategy is reported.

The 'automatic, reproducible' framing oversells: task templates, meta-path patterns, the three-tier pattern-priority strategy, and the seed/meta-path taxonomy are all hand-designed and hand-curated, so scaling to new domains requires nontrivial human engineering.

Novelty is moderate: representing webpages/documents as graphs and templating tasks over them is a natural composition of known ideas (SoM-style DOM parsing, seed-driven crawling, meta-paths from KG literature, MMR selection); the contribution is primarily a well-engineered system plus benchmark rather than a new methodological insight. The project page placeholder is also empty, and no explicit code/data release is stated, limiting reproducibility.
